content: Two fragments of glass and a small iron spike were discovered. Additionally, three shards of Roman pottery and ten shards of La Tène pottery were recovered from the site. The contemporaneity of Rome’s Imperial period, traditionally dated to the 1st–3rd century AD, with the Early Middle Ages (8th–10th century AD) has also been confirmed in Poland. In this region, the Late La Tène period (conventionally ending in the 1st century BC) directly precedes the Early Medieval period of the 8th–10th centuries AD. In the capital cities of Rome and Constantinople, residential quarters, streets, latrines, aqueducts, and ports were constructed during only one of three periods: Imperial Antiquity, Late Antiquity, or the Early Middle Ages, spanning from 1 to 930 AD. In Rome, these constructions are attributed to the Imperial Antiquity period (1st–3rd century AD), while in Constantinople, they are assigned to Late Antiquity (4th–6th century AD). Roman churches from Late Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages provide sufficient evidence to confirm the existence of these two periods. However, no churches from the 8th or 9th centuries are found superimposed on churches from the 4th or 5th centuries, which themselves are not superimposed on pagan basilicas from the 1st or 2nd centuries. Instead, all these structures share the same stratigraphic level, corresponding to the 1st and 2nd/early 3rd centuries. Furthermore, the ground plans of 4th/5th-century churches, as well as those from the 8th/9th centuries, closely replicate the layouts of 1st/2nd-century basilicas, a phenomenon noted 75 years ago by the scholar Richard Krautheimer (1897–1994). It is the period of Imperial Antiquity, with its internal evolution from the 1st to 3rd centuries, that is solely responsible for the construction of the residential quarters, latrines, streets, and aqueducts that are often sought in Late Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages. Consequently, Rome does not exhibit more stratigraphic evidence for the first millennium AD than England or Poland. Germanic tribes, including not only the Anglo-Saxons and Frisians but also the Franks, had been competing with Rome for control of the British Isles since the 1st century BC. Astonishingly, La Tène art styles, as noted by Hines (1996), dominate the pottery of the Saxons. The powerful La Tène Celts, under the rule of King Addedomaros of Camulodunum, were among the most significant rulers of this period. The Saxons began their incursions into Britain as early as the 1st century BC, competing with the Romans, who may have employed Germanic Franks as auxiliary forces. The Saxons invaded from the east, specifically from the German Bight. Stratigraphic evidence from the Saxon homeland, located around Bremen/Weser in modern-day Lower Saxony, indicates that the region was primarily inhabited by the Chauci and Bructeri tribes. These tribes were engaged in conflict with the Romans during the reign of Augustus (31 BC–14 AD) and the rule of Addedomaros of Camulodunum (circa 15–5 BC). On the right, an Indian-standard coin of King Maues is depicted. The obverse features a jubilant elephant holding a wreath, symbolizing victory, with the Greek inscription reading ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΝ ΜΕΓΑΛΟΥ ΜΑΥΟΥ (Great King of Kings Maues). The reverse shows the seated King Maues, accompanied by a Kharosthi inscription: RAJATIRAJASA MAHATASA MOASA (Great King of Kings Maues). Fragments of an ancient mechanism contain at least 30 interlocking gear wheels, along with extensive astronomical inscriptions. Before its submersion on the seabed, this device calculated and displayed the movements of the Sun, Moon, and possibly the planets around Earth, as well as predicted the dates of future eclipses. The Winged Nike of Samothrace, crafted from Parian marble, dates to approximately 190 BC. It was discovered in 1863 on the island of Samothrace by the archaeological expedition led by Charles Champoiseau. Cleopatra II, depicted on the left, was involved in the governance of Egypt from approximately 175 BC until her death in 116 BC. A survey diagram of a Sea Island, attributed to the Chinese mathematician Liu Hui during the Three Kingdoms era (220–280 CE), is an example of early cartographic and mathematical innovation. The Jastorf (La Tène) culture, characterized by its advanced bronze and iron technology, left behind significant architectural evidence in downtown Bremen. Many coins discovered at the submerged city of Heracleion date to the reign of King Ptolemy II, who ruled Egypt from 283 to 246 BC. Other finds include incomplete statues of the god Serapis and Queen Arsinoe II. Despite extensive efforts, no more than 5% of the city’s area has been explored by archaeologists. Edzná, a Mayan archaeological site in northern Campeche, Mexico, was already inhabited by 400 BC. The construction of the Parthenon in Athens began in 447 BC and was completed in 438 BC, with decorative work continuing until 432 BC. The historian Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BC, noted that the Temple of Heracles served as a sanctuary for runaway slaves. If a slave sought refuge there and bore the “sacred marks,” it was unlawful for their original owner to reclaim them. A map from the 6th century BC illustrates the regions of Assyria, Babylonia, and Armenia. Croesus, who ruled Lydia from 560 BC until his defeat by Cyrus the Great in 546 BC, issued gold-silver alloy coins. Based on pottery evidence, Croesus is believed to have been burned to death. Sappho of Eresos is depicted holding a lyre and plectrum, turning toward a bearded man with a partially visible lyre. An amulet dating from 800–612 BC was used to ward off plagues. Esarhaddon, portrayed on a stone stele dated after 671 BC, ruled Assyria between 681 and 669 BC. A black basalt monument narrates Esarhaddon’s restoration of Babylon around 670 BC. This artifact, originating from Babylon in Mesopotamia, is now housed in the British Museum, London. The Nimrud lens, a plano-convex artifact from the Neo-Assyrian period (750–710 BC), was discovered in the North West Palace of Nimrud by Austen Henry Layard in the 1850s. Known as the Loupe of Sargon, this rock-crystal lentoid is oval-shaped and uneven in thickness. The Dipylon Vase, dating to approximately 750 BC, represents the late Geometric or early Archaic period. A low-relief from the palace of Sargon II at Dur Sharrukin (modern-day Khorsabad, Iraq), dated to 716–713 BC, depicts scenes of Assyrian life. In the center is an image of the upper portion of a statue of Elissa, Queen of Carthage, dating to the early 8th or late 9th century BC. The founding of the Phoenician colony of Toscanos is dated to approximately 805–780 BC, based on radiocarbon analysis of its earliest strata. In 842 BC, the Kingdom of Israel and the Phoenician cities sent tributes to Shalmaneser III. The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III depicts King Jehu of Israel bowing before the Assyrian king. Carthage was founded in 814 BC, with radiocarbon dating confirming the timeline of its earliest levels.
